definition: To speak or argue in favor of an idea, plan, or cause.
example: Many doctors advocate regular exercise as a simple way to improve sleep.
nuance: To advocate is to argue openly for something, while to support can mean simply agreeing with it in private.
prompt: A nurse thinks her hospital needs more hand-washing stations in the hallways.
options: At the staff meeting, she will advocate adding three new stations near the patient rooms.
At the staff meeting, she will advocate the plan by insisting it would waste money.
Tired of long shifts, she decided to advocate her position and quit nursing.
She chose to advocate the idea by never mentioning it to anyone at work.
reasons: Arguing for the change in front of colleagues is exactly what this verb describes.
Calling a plan wasteful argues against it, which reverses the meaning.
This confuses the word with abdicate, which means to give up a role or duty.
The word implies speaking out; keeping an idea secret is not arguing for it.

practice.prompt: A student wishes the school library stayed open later on weeknights.
options: Maya wrote a letter to the principal to advocate longer evening hours.
Maya hoped to advocate later hours, so she asked that the library close at noon.
The principal will advocate the library budget evenly among the art and music clubs.
Maya tried to advocate the noisy library by studying at the kitchen table instead.
reasons: A persuasive letter to someone in charge is a clear way of arguing for a change.
Requesting earlier closing works against the goal instead of arguing for it.
This mixes up the word with allocate, which means to divide and hand out.
Staying away from a place is avoiding it, not speaking in favor of anything.
